system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
mechanism: Relative-risk framing can magnify the perceived effect of an intervention when baseline risk is small. Patient-centered risk communication presents baseline and treated absolute risks using the same denominator and time horizon, often alongside both benefit and harm information, so patients can judge the magnitude of effect.
vignette: A patient is considering a preventive medication. A clinical trial found that over 10 years, the outcome occurred in 2% of untreated participants and 1% of treated participants. The patient asks, “How much does this medicine actually change my chance of having the problem?”
lead: Which response best communicates the treatment benefit while minimizing misleading risk framing?
correct: “Over 10 years, about 2 of every 100 people without the medicine had the outcome, compared with about 1 of every 100 people who took it.”
distractors: “The medicine cuts your risk by 50%, so it prevents the problem in about half of people who take it.”
“The number needed to treat is 100, which is the most understandable way to describe the benefit.”
“The medication is very effective, and serious events are uncommon, so exact numbers are more likely to confuse you.”
“Your risk is reduced from 1 in 50 to 1 in 100, while the relative reduction is 50%; using different denominators makes the comparison more intuitive.”
distractor_notes: A 50% relative reduction is mathematically correct but, without baseline absolute risk, can exaggerate perceived benefit; it also incorrectly implies that half of treated people personally avoid the outcome.
NNT can be useful, but patient understanding is generally improved by providing absolute event rates; it should not replace baseline and treated risks as the only description.
Vague qualitative terms such as 'very effective' and 'uncommon' can be interpreted inconsistently and withhold relevant quantitative information.
The two fractions are mathematically equivalent to the correct absolute risks, but inconsistent denominators make comparison harder; same-denominator presentation is recommended.
key_expl: The most transparent response gives both baseline and treated absolute risks over the same time period and with the same denominator: 2 in 100 versus 1 in 100 over 10 years. Saying only that risk is reduced by 50% reports a relative risk reduction and can make a modest absolute change appear larger. Consistent denominators allow direct comparison, while numerical risk information is preferable to vague terms such as 'rare' or 'very effective.'
objective: Communicate treatment effects using absolute risks with the same denominator and time horizon rather than relying on relative-risk framing alone.
clues: patient asks about magnitude of personal benefit

sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.title: SHARE Approach Workshop — Module 3: Communication
sources.locator: Module 3, slide 48–49 guidance on conveying health numbers
sources.support: AHRQ recommends giving absolute rather than relative risk, using concrete event counts, framing outcomes in both positive and negative terms, and using visuals when useful.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Shared decision making
sources.date: Current NCBI Bookshelf guideline page verified 2026-08-27
sources.support: The guideline recommends numerical risk data, absolute rather than relative risk, natural frequencies, consistent denominators, defined time periods, and balanced framing.

sources.title: Communicating data about the benefits and harms of treatment: a randomized trial
sources.support: The randomized trial supports explicit presentation of absolute benefits and harms and shows that comprehension depends on numeric format, cautioning against unsupported claims that one format is universally superior.
